## Why the best teams win

The model trained on 256 knockout team-seasons demonstrates a mean within-season Spearman correlation of 0.46 between predicted and actual stages, with an AUC for reaching the final of 0.72. Its Brier score is 0.098 compared to a base-rate guess of 0.103, indicating a marginal improvement in predictive accuracy without statistical significance testing. In 46.7% of seasons, actual finalists appeared within the model's top four predictions. The feature-set comparison reveals that style-based stats yield the highest individual performance with a Spearman correlation of 0.41 and an AUC of 0.69, while the pedigree set achieves only 0.28 and 0.66 respectively. Combining all features results in a Spearman of 0.47 when pedigree is removed, suggesting style and results drive the association more than reputation alone.

Among individual stats, Attacks per game carries an importance of 0.25 knockout stages, making it the most significant predictor, followed by Goal difference per game at 0.201. Both are marked as robust across seasons. Long passes (% of passes) and Passes per game follow with importances of 0.137 and 0.128 respectively, also labeled robust. Conversely, Fouls committed per game has an importance of 0.088 but is model-dependent, while Shot conversion shows a negative direction with an importance of 0.086 yet remains robust. Distance covered per game ranks lower at 0.077 and lacks a robustness label. These findings indicate that deep runs are statistically associated with high-volume attacking styles and strong goal differentials rather than historical pedigree, though the model's edge over the base-rate guess was not tested for significance.

## Winners vs runners-up

A comparison of group/league-phase stats between winners and runners-up across 15 finals shows no differences that meet the Holm-adjusted p-value threshold of 0.05. Pre-season UEFA club coefficient had a mean difference z-score of 0.57 with a p-value of 0.111, while Fouls committed per game showed a negative direction with a z-score of -1.13 and a p-value of 0.181. Shots per game displayed a winner advantage in 11 finals versus 2 losses, yet the mean difference z-score of 0.79 resulted in a p-value of 0.292. Pass accuracy and Passes per game both showed winners higher in 12 instances with p-values of 0.422, but these remain non-significant. Points per game was perfectly balanced with 7 wins and 7 losses for the winner category, yielding a mean difference z-score of -0.01 and a p-value of 1.0.

Goal difference per game saw winners higher in 9 finals against 4 lower results, but the mean difference z-score of 0.22 produced a p-value of 1.0. Shot accuracy and Shot conversion also failed to reach significance with p-values of 1.0 despite varying counts of winner-higher outcomes. Attacks per game had winners higher in 11 finals versus 4 lower, resulting in a mean difference z-score of 0.9 but a p-value of 1.0 due to the Holm adjustment. Defensive metrics like Opponent shots per game and Opponent shots on target per game showed no significant separation with p-values of 1.0. Possession favored winners in 9 finals, yet the mean difference z-score of 0.5 yielded a p-value of 1.0. Long passes and Distance covered per game also resulted in non-significant differences with p-values of 1.0. Consequently, no single stat significantly distinguishes winners from runners-up based on pre-season or league-phase data alone.

Quote every number exactly as it appears in the facts, with the same rounding. Do not introduce players, managers, matches, events, analyses or numbers that are not in the facts. 'Teams beaten (%)' figures say how many teams the club did better than on a stat, so higher is always better, including for stats marked '(lower is better)', where doing better means having the lower value. Write them as 'better than X% of teams', never as 'top X%'. SHAP contributions are measured in knockout stages: a positive contribution means the stat pushed the model's expected stage up by that fraction of a round, a negative one pushed it down. A SHAP contribution is the model's view, not a measure of how good the team was at the stat: a team can rank high on a stat the model marked down, so never call a stat a strength or a weakness because of its SHAP sign. Everything here is a statistical association, not a cause: never say a stat or a team's profile drove, powered, propelled, carried, helped, hindered or prevented a result, and do not explain why a stat got its contribution. Use 'significant' or 'significantly' only for a Holm-adjusted p-value comparison, never for other differences. Write plain markdown without tables.

Write 350-450 words of markdown in total, two paragraphs of about 100 words under each of exactly these two headings, in this order:
## Why the best teams win
## Winners vs runners-up

Explain which stats are associated with deep knockout runs and whether pedigree, results or style matters most, using the feature-set comparison. Say how well the model does by comparing its Brier score with the base-rate Brier score and stating how often finalists were in its top 4; the model's edge over the base-rate guess was not tested, so do not call it significant or superior. 'Importance' is the average size of a stat's push on the expected stage, in either direction. The model learns from the knockout team-seasons, using each team's group/league-phase stats. Report findings only: do not explain how SHAP or the model works. Only call a stat 'robust' if its robustness label is robust. Winners vs runners-up compares those same group/league-phase stats, not what happened in the final. Never call a winners-vs-runners-up difference significant unless its Holm-adjusted p is below the significance threshold in the facts.
